phase1.intro:
🎉 Nice work — that's the whole of Unit 2 in the books! Let's walk back through everything, since this is exactly the kind of unit where the ideas build directly on each other.

Where do you want to start the recap?

topics.buttonText: How did inheritance and polymorphism connect?
dialogue: We started with [[term:inheritance]] — `extends`, the IS-A relationship, `super` reaching up to the parent. From there, [[term:overriding]] let a subclass swap out a parent's behavior entirely.

[[key:Runtime polymorphism]] meant Java decides which version actually runs based on the object's real type — the same idea whether it's overriding OR the overloading (compile-time polymorphism) you already knew from Unit 1.

stickyNote.flavor: 🔗 extends, override, and two flavors of polymorphism
stickyNote.definition: Inheritance (extends, IS-A, super) enables overriding, which enables runtime polymorphism — the object's real type deciding which method runs.

topics.buttonText: How do abstract classes and interfaces differ again?
dialogue: Then we opened up two ways to build "incomplete-on-purpose" blueprints: [[term:abstract classes]], which can hold real state and force subclasses to fill in specific methods, and [[term:interfaces]], pure contracts that a class can sign as many of as it wants — including default and static methods since Java 8.

stickyNote.definition: Abstract classes hold shared state and force method implementation. Interfaces are pure contracts, implementable in any number, with default/static methods.

topics.buttonText: What were the supporting tools, and what's next?
dialogue: The rest of the unit filled in supporting tools: packages, static members, final, inner classes, enums, Object's toString()/equals()/hashCode(), and wrapper classes. [[key:Here's the thread connecting all of it]]: every tool in this unit is really about controlling how much one piece of code can assume about, depend on, or be replaced by another.

What's next? [[key:Design patterns]] — proven, reusable shapes for solving common structural problems. One idea worth planting early: [[warn:composition over inheritance]] — favoring "has-a" relationships over "is-a" ones often keeps code more flexible and easier to test.

stickyNote.flavor: 🧵 controlling coupling, heading toward design patterns
stickyNote.definition: Unit 2's tools all control how tightly classes couple to each other. Next up: design patterns, starting with the idea of composition over inheritance.

phase1.openingDialogue: Unit 2 in a nutshell: inheritance and polymorphism, two flavors of incomplete blueprints, and the supporting tools that control coupling. 🎉

phase2.explanation:
No broken code this time — but there's a genuine misconception worth clearing up before we move on: [[warn:"inheritance is always the best way to reuse code"]] isn't actually true, and a lot of experienced Java developers will tell you composition is often the better default.

[[key:Composition just means giving a class a field that IS another object, instead of extending it]] — `class Car { Engine engine; }` instead of `class Car extends Engine`. The composed version is usually more flexible: you can swap which Engine a Car uses at runtime, you're not locked into Engine's entire public interface whether you want all of it or not, and it tends to be much easier to test in isolation.

[[key:This is exactly the kind of judgment call design patterns exist to help you make]] — not "which keyword is correct," but "which relationship between these two classes will actually serve the code best."

phase3.openingDialogue: Final check! Which of these do you know? 🤔

mcq.question:
Which statement about OOP concepts is TRUE?

A) A class can extend multiple classes (multiple inheritance)
B) Interfaces can have concrete methods using default keyword (Java 8+)
C) Abstract classes can't have constructors
D) The equals() method compares object references by default
E) Static methods can access instance variables
F) final classes can be extended

Select the CORRECT statement.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: "design patterns" as a formal concept in software really took off after a single 1994 book — often just called "the Gang of Four book" after its four authors — which catalogued 23 recurring solutions to common object-oriented design problems. Strategy, the pattern mentioned above, is one of the original 23.
phase5.openingDialogue: Unit 2 done — one more thought before Unit 3~
